variants.name: Broker-enforced TTL with dead-lettering on expiration
variants.implementation_notes: On the .NET cloud-messaging path expiry is declared, not coded: ServiceBusMessage.TimeToLive overrides the entity default for one message, and with DeadLetteringOnMessageExpiration enabled the broker moves expired messages to the dead-letter sub-queue with reason TTLExpiredException instead of dropping them silently. Message and entity TTL interact - the earliest wins, and a message asking for longer is silently shortened to the entity default - while a message locked for delivery does not expire at all, so a handler that must not act on stale data still re-checks the deadline it cares about. MSMQ's TimeToBeReceived is the on-premises equivalent of the same idea.
pitfalls: Entity-level TTL caps per-message TTL: a message asking for a longer lifetime is silently shortened, and nothing surfaces that unless someone inspects the dead-letter queue or the entity configuration.
A locked (in-flight) message does not expire while locked, and TTL is not evaluated once a message is in the DLQ, so expiry is suspended exactly where stale work can still be processed.
TimeToLive is inspected in the handler only if you read it: Service Bus will not revoke a message it already delivered, so long-running handlers need their own deadline check.

variants.name: Runtime deadline via CancellationTokenSource.CancelAfter
variants.idiom_name: CancellationTokenSource.CancelAfter plus a UTC deadline on the work item
variants.implementation_notes: For in-process queues the BCL supplies the pattern directly: CancelAfter(TimeSpan) flips the token when the deadline elapses, so awaiting consumers abandon the work, and the work item carries its own absolute deadline (DateTimeOffset.UtcNow plus the TTL, or a TimeProvider timestamp) that the handler re-checks before side effects. This replaces the broker with cancellation, which is cheaper and easy to test; it only protects work that is still awaiting, so a handler that blocks synchronously or ignores the token keeps running. Prefer it for Channel<T> and actor-loop mailboxes inside one process, and keep broker TTL when the message crosses a process boundary.
pitfalls: CancelAfter only signals: a handler that ignores the token, blocks on synchronous I/O, or catches OperationCanceledException and continues still runs past the deadline.

DateTimeOffset.UtcNow is a settable wall clock, so NTP steps shift every deadline; inject TimeProvider (or compare Environment.TickCount64 for local elapsed time) and keep the serialized form an absolute UTC value.
One shared CancellationTokenSource for many messages cancels them all when the first expires; each item needs its own deadline or a timer per deadline bucket.
